assessments.explanation: `strptime` doesn't know or care what order a date string was 'meant' to be in -- it purely follows the format string's positions, character for character. `"%d/%m/%Y"` tells it to read the first number as the day, the second as the month, and the third as the year. Both `03` and `04` happen to be structurally valid for either a day or a month, so parsing succeeds without any error -- it's just that `parsed.day` ends up as `3` and `parsed.month` ends up as `4`, the reverse of what was intended (March 4th). This is a genuinely dangerous failure mode: strptime is unforgiving about *structural* mismatches (raising ValueError when the string's punctuation or digit-count doesn't fit the format), but it has no way to catch a *semantic* mismatch like this one, where the format string is structurally compatible but assigns the wrong meaning to each field.

concepts.title: Regular Expressions
concepts.description: The re module matches text against patterns, but match, search, and findall behave differently in a way that trips people up constantly, and raw strings are almost always the right way to write the patterns themselves.
learningObjectives: Distinguish re.match, re.search, and re.findall, and explain precisely why match only succeeds when a pattern matches at the very start of the string.
Read and write common regex building blocks: character classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups.
Explain why raw strings (r"...") are almost always used for regex patterns, and predict what goes wrong without them.
Evaluate when a regex is the right tool for a text-matching problem versus when it hurts readability more than it helps.

sections.heading: match vs search vs findall: The Recurring Point of Confusion
sections.body:
Python's `re` module offers several functions for applying a pattern to a string, and three of them are confused constantly, specifically because their names all sound like they should do roughly the same thing:

- **`re.match(pattern, string)`** checks for a match **only at the very beginning** of the string. If the pattern would match somewhere in the *middle* of the string but not starting at position 0, `match` returns `None` -- it does not search further in.
- **`re.search(pattern, string)`** scans through the *entire* string, looking for the *first* location anywhere where the pattern matches -- this is what most people intuitively expect 'find a match' to mean.
- **`re.findall(pattern, string)`** finds **every non-overlapping** occurrence of the pattern anywhere in the string, and returns them all as a list.

```python
import re

text = "The year 2026 was great, and 2027 looks good too."

print(re.match(r"\d+", text))     # None -- the string doesn't START with digits
print(re.search(r"\d+", text))    # <re.Match object; span=(9, 13), match='2026'> -- found it, mid-string
print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))   # ['2026', '2027'] -- every match, as plain strings
```

`re.match` returning `None` here is not a bug or a surprise once you know the rule -- the string literally does not begin with a digit (it begins with `"The year..."`), so a pattern anchored implicitly to the start correctly fails to match. The single most common mistake with this module is reaching for `re.match` when you actually mean 'does this pattern appear anywhere in the string,' getting an unexpected `None`, and not realizing `match`'s start-anchoring is the reason. If you want 'somewhere in the string,' `search` (for the first match) or `findall` (for all matches) is almost always what you actually want; reach for `match` specifically when you genuinely need to validate that a string *starts with* a particular pattern (parsing a fixed-format prefix, for instance).

sections.heading: Common Building Blocks
sections.body:
A working vocabulary of a handful of regex building blocks covers most everyday pattern-matching needs:

- **Character classes**: `\d` (any digit, equivalent to `[0-9]`), `\w` (any 'word' character: letters, digits, underscore), `\s` (any whitespace), and their uppercase negations `\D`, `\W`, `\S` (anything *not* matching the lowercase version). `[abc]` matches any one of `a`, `b`, or `c`; `[^abc]` matches any character *except* those.
- **Quantifiers**: `*` (zero or more), `+` (one or more), `?` (zero or one -- 'optional'), `{n}` (exactly n), `{n,m}` (between n and m, inclusive).
- **Anchors**: `^` (start of string, or start of line in multiline mode), `$` (end of string, or end of line in multiline mode).
- **Groups**: parentheses `(...)` capture a sub-part of the match for later extraction (via `.group(1)`, etc.), and `|` inside or around a group means 'or' (alternation).

```python
import re

match = re.search(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.com", "Contact: amy@example.com for help")
if match:
    print(match.group(0))   # 'amy@example.com' -- the whole match
    print(match.group(1))   # 'amy'              -- first parenthesized group
    print(match.group(2))   # 'example'           -- second parenthesized group
```

This pattern reads as: one-or-more word characters (captured), literal `@`, one-or-more word characters (captured), a literal dot, then `com`. Groups let you pull out the specific pieces you care about (the username, the domain) rather than just knowing *that* something matched.

sections.heading: Raw Strings: Why You Almost Always Want r"..."
sections.body:
Regex patterns use backslash (`\`) heavily as an escape character for its own special sequences (`\d`, `\w`, `\s`, `\.`  for a literal dot, and so on). Python's *own* string literals also use backslash as an escape character, for entirely different purposes (`\n` for newline, `\t` for tab). When these two backslash-escaping systems collide inside an ordinary string literal, the result is confusing, and sometimes silently wrong rather than a clean error:

```python
import re

# Without a raw string: '\d' isn't a recognized Python escape sequence,
# so Python leaves it as a literal backslash + d (with a DeprecationWarning in modern Python) --
# this particular case happens to still work, but it's fragile and relies on a coincidence
pattern_risky = "\d+"

# '\b' IS a recognized Python escape sequence (backspace, \x08) -- a genuine collision
pattern_broken = "\bfoo"   # NOT the regex 'word boundary + foo' -- this is a literal backspace character + 'foo'

# The fix: raw strings disable Python's own backslash escaping entirely,
# so what you write is exactly what the regex engine sees
pattern_correct = r"\bfoo"   # a literal backslash, then 'b', then 'foo' -- exactly what regex \b means

print(re.search(pattern_broken, "a footnote"))    # None -- looking for an actual backspace character!
print(re.search(pattern_correct, "a footnote"))   # None too, actually -- but for the RIGHT reason (see below)
print(re.search(pattern_correct, "a foo bar"))    # matches 'foo' -- \b (word boundary) works correctly here
```

A **raw string**, written with an `r` prefix (`r"..."`), tells Python's parser to treat every backslash inside it literally -- `\b` inside a raw string is genuinely the two characters backslash-then-b, with none of Python's own escape processing applied, and it's the regex engine, not Python's string parser, that then interprets `\b` as 'word boundary.' Without the raw string, you're at the mercy of a coincidence: some regex escape sequences (like `\d`) happen to not collide with any Python string escape, so they pass through unchanged (though modern Python versions emit a `DeprecationWarning` for this, since it's fragile and unintended), while others (like `\b`, `\n`, `\t`) collide directly with a real Python escape sequence and get silently transformed into something completely different before the regex engine ever sees them. The practical rule: **always** write regex patterns as raw strings, `r"..."` -- there is essentially never a good reason not to, and it eliminates an entire category of confusing, sometimes-silent bugs at zero cost.

sections.heading: An Honest Note on Readability
sections.body:
Regular expressions are genuinely powerful -- a single pattern can express matching logic that would otherwise take many lines of manual string manipulation. That power comes at a real cost: a sufficiently complex regex is famously difficult to read back later, including by the person who wrote it a few weeks prior. `^(?:[a-zA-Z0-9_.+-]+)@(?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}$` is a plausible-looking, largely-functional email-matching pattern, and it is close to unreadable at a glance.

The practical, honest guidance: reach for a regex when the problem genuinely calls for pattern matching (validating a format, extracting structured pieces from semi-structured text, splitting on a pattern rather than a fixed delimiter) rather than for problems better solved by plain string methods (`.split()`, `.startswith()`, `"x" in s`) -- if a plain string method solves the problem clearly, prefer it; it's more readable and usually faster. And when a regex genuinely is the right tool, especially for anything beyond the simplest patterns, **write a comment explaining what it matches and why**, in plain language -- future readers (including future you) should not need to mentally re-derive a non-trivial pattern character by character just to understand what a piece of code is checking for. Python's `re.VERBOSE` flag, which lets you write a pattern spread across multiple lines with inline comments and ignored whitespace, is also worth knowing about specifically for this reason -- it turns an otherwise-dense one-liner into something considerably more maintainable.

examples.title: match's Start-Anchoring vs search's Full Scan
examples.code:
import re

log_line = "[INFO] Server started successfully"

# match fails: the string doesn't START with 'Server'
print(re.match(r"Server", log_line))    # None

# search succeeds: 'Server' appears somewhere in the string
print(re.search(r"Server", log_line))    # <re.Match object; span=(7, 13), match='Server'>

# match succeeds here: the string DOES start with '[INFO]'
print(re.match(r"\[INFO\]", log_line))    # <re.Match object; span=(0, 6), match='[INFO]'>

# Using match correctly: validating that a log line starts with a recognized level tag
for level in ["INFO", "WARN", "ERROR"]:
    if re.match(rf"\[{level}\]", log_line):
        print(f"This line's level is: {level}")
        break
examples.explanation: re.match(r"Server", log_line) returns None specifically because 'Server' appears starting at index 7, not index 0 -- match only ever considers a match starting exactly at the beginning of the string, so it never gets a chance to look further in, no matter how obviously present the pattern is elsewhere. re.search finds it because search scans the whole string for the first place the pattern matches, regardless of position. The final loop shows match used appropriately: since log lines in this format genuinely are expected to start with a bracketed level tag, checking 'does this line start with [INFO]' is precisely what match is suited for -- it's a validation of the string's beginning, not a general 'is this pattern present somewhere' search.

examples.title: The Raw String Collision, Concretely
examples.code:
import re

text = "Section 1\tTitle\nSection 2\tIntro"

# Intending to match a tab character between a number and the following word
pattern_no_raw = "\tTitle"      # Python turns \t into an actual TAB character before regex even sees it
pattern_raw = r"\tTitle"         # regex engine sees the two characters \ and t, and interprets THAT as tab too

print(re.search(pattern_no_raw, text))   # matches -- \t means tab to BOTH Python strings and regex, so this coincidentally works
print(re.search(pattern_raw, text))       # also matches -- r"\t" is interpreted by the regex engine's OWN \t handling

# Where it actually breaks: \b means something completely different to Python strings (backspace) vs regex (word boundary)
print(re.search("\bTitle", text))    # None -- Python already turned \b into a literal backspace char before regex ran
print(re.search(r"\bTitle", text))    # matches -- regex correctly sees \b as 'word boundary', then 'Title'
examples.explanation: \t happens to mean 'tab' to both Python's string literal parser AND to the regex engine, so pattern_no_raw and pattern_raw behave identically here purely by coincidence -- this is exactly the trap, because it can make it look like raw strings 'don't matter' until you hit an escape sequence where the two systems disagree. \b is exactly that case: to Python's own string parser, \b is the backspace control character (\x08), so "\bTitle" has already been silently transformed into an actual backspace character followed by 'Title' before the regex engine ever sees it -- there's no 'word boundary' left in the pattern by the time re.search runs, hence the failed match. r"\bTitle", by contrast, is passed to the regex engine as the literal two characters backslash-b followed by 'Title', which is exactly what the regex engine's own \b (word boundary) syntax expects, so it matches correctly.

examples.title: When findall and Groups Do the Real Work
examples.code:
import re

log = """
2026-08-14 09:15 ERROR Connection timeout
2026-08-14 09:16 INFO Retry succeeded
2026-08-14 09:20 ERROR Connection timeout
"""

# Extract just the timestamps of every ERROR line
error_times = re.findall(r"(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}) ERROR", log)
print(error_times)   # ['2026-08-14 09:15', '2026-08-14 09:20']
examples.explanation: The pattern breaks down as: a date (\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}), a space, a time (\d{2}:\d{2}), all wrapped in one capturing group, followed by a literal space and the word ERROR (not itself captured, since it's outside the parentheses). findall returns exactly the captured group's content for every match -- not the full match including 'ERROR' -- because when a pattern contains exactly one group, findall returns a list of just that group's matches rather than full match strings. This is a realistic, common regex use case: pulling structured pieces of information (here, just the timestamps of a specific category of log line) out of semi-structured text, which would be considerably more verbose to do with manual string splitting and conditionals.

misconceptions.description: re.match(pattern, text) checks whether the pattern appears anywhere in text -- the same as re.search.
misconceptions.clarification: re.match only ever considers a match that starts at position 0 of the string -- if the pattern would match starting anywhere else, match returns None regardless of how clearly present the pattern is elsewhere in the string. re.search is the function that scans the entire string for the first position, anywhere, where the pattern matches. This is the single most common source of confusion with the re module -- reaching for match when search (or findall, for multiple matches) is what's actually needed, and getting an unexpected None as a result with no indication of why.

misconceptions.description: Writing regex patterns as raw strings (r"...") is just a stylistic convention -- it doesn't change what the pattern actually matches.
misconceptions.clarification: Raw strings can and do change behavior, not just style, whenever a pattern includes a backslash sequence that Python's own string literal syntax also recognizes as something else. \b is the clearest example: inside an ordinary (non-raw) string, Python's parser converts \b into an actual backspace control character before the regex engine ever runs, silently destroying the intended 'word boundary' meaning -- the pattern still runs without any error, it just matches something different (or nothing at all) than intended. \n and \t behave similarly. Some regex escapes, like \d, happen to not collide with any Python string escape and pass through unchanged either way (though modern Python emits a DeprecationWarning for relying on this), which is exactly what makes the misconception plausible -- it works by coincidence often enough to seem harmless, right up until a pattern includes one of the escapes that actually collides.

Prefixing the pattern with r fixes the underlying fragility regardless of which escape sequences are used, and is the correct habit to build regardless of whether a specific pattern's escapes happen to survive unharmed today; a pattern that later gets extended to include \b (word boundary) or a literal \n, without also being made raw, would silently break in a way this specific pattern does not.

assessments.prompt: A teammate submits a pull request with the regex pattern "\d{3}\b\w+" (not a raw string) to validate part number formats, and asks you to review it. Explain the risk in how the pattern is written, and how you'd advise them to fix it -- even if it happens to work correctly on their test cases today.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core risk is that the pattern is written as an ordinary Python string literal rather than a raw string, which means Python's own string parser processes any backslash escape sequences in it BEFORE the regex engine ever sees the pattern. Some regex escapes, like \d, happen to not correspond to any recognized Python string escape sequence, so Python leaves them alone (with a DeprecationWarning in modern versions, since this reliance is considered fragile) -- which is exactly why this pattern might appear to work fine on their test cases today. But \b is a real, recognized Python string escape sequence, meaning to the string literal, not to the regex engine: it represents the backspace control character (\x08). By the time this string reaches re.match or re.search, the \b the teammate intended as a regex 'word boundary' has already been silently converted into a literal backspace character -- the pattern no longer contains a word boundary assertion at all, it contains an actual backspace byte, which will essentially never appear in real input text, meaning this part of the pattern will likely never match anything as intended, probably causing this regex to fail to match cases it should. Passing their existing test cases doesn't rule this out -- it just means their tests happen not to exercise the specific situation where the word-boundary behavior actually matters. The fix is straightforward and should always be applied to regex patterns as a blanket habit, not just when a bug is suspected: write the pattern as a raw string, r"\d{3}\b\w+", which disables Python's own backslash processing entirely, so \b (and every other escape in the pattern) reaches the regex engine exactly as written and is interpreted purely by regex's own rules.

assessments.prompt:
```python
import re

text = "file_final_v2.txt"
result = re.search(r"v\d+\.txt$", text)
print(result.group() if result else None)

text2 = "file_final_v2.txt.bak"
result2 = re.search(r"v\d+\.txt$", text2)
print(result2.group() if result2 else None)
```
What gets printed?
options: v2.txt then None
v2.txt then v2.txt
None then v2.txt
v2.txt.bak then v2.txt.bak
assessments.explanation: `$` anchors the pattern to the *end* of the string -- the match must finish exactly where the string finishes. `text` genuinely ends in `"v2.txt"`, so `v\d+\.txt$` matches there, giving `"v2.txt"`. `text2` ends in `".bak"`, not `".txt"` -- even though `"v2.txt"` appears in the middle of `text2`, the pattern's `$` anchor requires the match to reach the actual end of the string, which it can't, since more characters (`.bak`) follow it. So `re.search` correctly returns no match for `text2`, and the second line prints `None`. This is exactly what `$` is for: matching something specifically at the end, not merely 'somewhere in' the string.
